title: Scoping Rules in R
objectives: Explain lexical scoping and environment parent chains.
Trace name lookup through local and enclosing environments.

traps: R uses lexical scoping: lookup follows the function's creation environment, not simply its caller.

scenes.title: An environment stores named bindings
body: An environment maps names to objects and has a parent. Lookup starts in the current evaluation environment and follows parent links until the first matching binding is found. A nearer binding masks a same-named binding farther up the chain.

refresh: R begins by checking the environment in which the expression is currently evaluated. If the name is absent, it follows the parent link to the next environment and continues outward. This ordered search is the basis of lexical name resolution, and it stops as soon as a matching binding is found.

An environment is more than a list of variable names: it stores bindings from names to objects and records a parent environment. The parent relationship forms a chain that R follows when a name is not found locally. To solve exam traces, write the environments in order and mark the first one containing the requested name.

items.recall: A nearer binding hides a same-named parent binding.
refresh: A binding in the current environment takes precedence over a same-named binding in a parent environment. The parent value is not deleted or overwritten; it is simply masked for this lookup. When the local environment is no longer the active evaluation context, the parent binding can be visible again.

scenes.title: The caller does not control lexical lookup
body: A function remembers the environment in which it was created. That is its enclosing environment. Its calling environment is where it was invoked. R follows the enclosing chain for free variables; the caller's local bindings are not automatically searched.

scenario.title: A function called from a temporary workspace
body: A pricing function is created in an environment where tax_rate=0.05. Later, another function is called from a temporary workspace where tax_rate=0.10. The pricing function refers to tax_rate but does not receive it as an argument and does not create a local binding with that name. The two values are deliberately different so that the lookup rule can be observed.

R uses lexical scoping. The function remembers the environment in which it was created, and that environment is the starting point for resolving its free variables after local arguments and assignments are checked. The caller's temporary tax_rate is not automatically inserted into this lookup chain, so it cannot replace the function's enclosing binding.
scenario.q: Which tax_rate is found if no nearer binding exists?

scenes.title: Trace lexical scoping in nested calls
scenes.problem: Global x=10. Define g=function() x. Define f=function(){x=20; g()}. Calling f() returns 10: g was created globally, so its lexical lookup finds global x. f's local x is only in g's calling environment.

steps.why: The function retains its creation environment.

steps.math: f's local x=20 is in the caller, not g's lexical parent.
steps.why: Lexical lookup does not use the caller's local variables.

steps.math: g finds global x=10; f() returns 10.
steps.why: The first matching binding in g's enclosing chain is global x.

scenes.problem: Global score=80. Evaluate f=function(){score=25; score+5}. The local score becomes 25, so f() returns 30. The global score remains 80 because ordinary assignment acted in the function evaluation environment.

scenes.title: Trace <<- through nested environments
scenes.problem: Global level=1. outer=function(){level=2; inner=function(){level <<- 9}; inner(); level}. inner was created inside outer, so <<- finds outer's local level first. outer() returns 9; global level remains 1.
hints: Identify the function's local environment and its enclosing environment.
Find the first matching binding along the relevant chain.
Evaluate the final expression after applying the assignment rule.
scenes.check: The first matching binding in the lexical environment chain is the one used or updated.

solution.math: outer's evaluation environment contains level = 2; its parent, .GlobalEnv, contains level = 1.
solution.why: The local and global bindings are distinct; the nearer outer binding is the first match.

solution.math: inner's enclosing environment is outer's evaluation environment. level <<- 9 updates that binding from 2 to 9.
solution.why: <<- starts searching in the parent of inner's evaluation environment and updates the first existing binding.

solution.math: The final expression reads outer's level = 9. Thus outer() returns 9, while global level remains 1.
solution.why: The update changed the enclosing local binding, not the global binding.

scenario.title: A counter retained by a closure
body: A factory function creates a local variable named counter and then returns an inner function. The inner function uses counter <<- counter+1 and then returns counter. The factory has already finished executing by the time the learner calls the returned function several times, so the example tests whether the inner function retains access to its creation environment.

The returned inner function is a closure: it retains its enclosing environment while it remains reachable. The counter binding is stored in that retained environment, and superassignment searches outward from the inner function's evaluation environment to find and update it. Each call therefore sees the value left by the previous call, even though the factory call has returned.
scenario.q: Why can the returned function still access counter?
scenario.answer: It retains the factory environment as its enclosing environment.

blocks.body: A closure is a function plus its enclosing environment. make_counter=function(){n=0; function(){n <<- n+1; n}} returns an inner function that retains the environment containing n. Calls return 1, then 2, then 3.

scenes.title: The scoping exam checklist
body: R uses lexical scoping. Lookup starts locally and follows parent environments. The function's enclosing environment is where it was created, not where it was called. <- normally creates a local binding. <<- searches outward and updates the first match, or falls back to .GlobalEnv. Closures retain their enclosing environments.
